fields.Front: APPLICATION (Elmasri exercise 3.27): give a cardinality ratio for each pair and state your assumption - (a) STUDENT / SOCIAL_SECURITY_CARD, (b) COURSE / TEXTBOOK, (c) CLASS / INSTRUCTOR, (d) EBAY_AUCTION_ITEM / EBAY_BID, (e) CLASSROOM / WALL.
fields.Back:
(a) 1:1 - one card per student and one student per card.
(b) M:N - a course may adopt several texts and a text may be used in several courses.
(c) N:1 - a class has one instructor and an instructor teaches many classes (M:N if team teaching is allowed).
(d) 1:N - an auction item receives many bids and a bid is for one item.
(e) 1:N - a classroom has many walls and a wall belongs to one room (M:N if shared walls are modelled).
The point of the exercise: the ratio comes from the MEANING OF THE MINIWORLD and from the assumptions you state - the instructor's 'this all depends on the context'.

fields.Text: Textbook (Elmasri §3.7.4, §3.8): NOTATION CONFLICT - this course and the textbook place a (min, max) pair {{c1::beside the entity it constrains}}, so its max matches the Chen letter at the opposite end of the line; {{c1::UML}} class diagrams place the same numbers, which they call {{c1::multiplicities}}, at the opposite end. Crow's Foot symbols are also read at the far end.

Textbook (Elmasri §3.9.1): three binary relationships CAN_SUPPLY, USES and SUPPLIES are {{c1::not}} equivalent to the ternary SUPPLY, because instances (s,p), (j,p) and (s,j) do not imply that {{c1::(s, j, p)}} exists. A ternary can instead be modelled as a weak entity with {{c1::three owners}} and no partial key, or as a regular entity given a surrogate key.
